title: U.S. House · Arkansas's 2nd District
area: Central Arkansas, including Little Rock, North Little Rock, and Conway.

context.text: Incumbent French Hill defeated Chase McDowell in the March 3, 2026 Republican primary. Chris Jones defeated Zack Huffman in the Democratic primary. Jones previously ran for Arkansas Governor in 2022, losing to Sarah Huckabee Sanders.

summary.text: French Hill is the Republican nominee and incumbent U.S. Representative for Arkansas's 2nd District, seeking re-election. A Little Rock banker and former Treasury Department and White House official, he has served in the House since January 2015 and chairs the House Financial Services Committee in the 119th Congress.

background.text: According to his official House biography, he is a ninth-generation Arkansan who lives in Little Rock with his wife, Martha; they have a daughter and a son.
Earned a bachelor's degree from Vanderbilt University in 1975; his House biography says he graduated magna cum laude in economics.
From 1982 to 1984 he served on the staff of U.S. Senator John Tower (R-TX) and on the staff of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

Served as Deputy Assistant Secretary of the U.S. Treasury for Corporate Finance (1989-1991) under President George H.W. Bush, then as senior policy advisor and Executive Secretary of the President's Economic Policy Council (1991-1993); he received the Treasury Department's Distinguished Service Award in January 1993.

Worked in investments and banking for about three decades; he was founder, chairman and chief executive officer of Delta Trust & Banking Corporation from 1999 until it was sold to Simmons Bank in 2014.
Worked as a senior advisor to Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee in 2008.
Civic roles include past president of the Rotary Club of Little Rock and 2013 chairman of the Little Rock Regional Chamber of Commerce.
Won the 2014 election to the U.S. House, succeeding Tim Griffin (R), and took office January 3, 2015.

In the 118th Congress he was Vice Chairman of the House Financial Services Committee and chaired its subcommittee on digital assets and financial technology; he has chaired the full committee in the 119th Congress.

As chairman, he led the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law on July 11, 2026 after passing the Senate 85-14 and the House 358-32, and his Main Street Capital Access Act (H.R. 6955) passed the House 270-155-1 on July 21, 2026.

priorities.text: It cuts red tape, increases housing supply, and makes homeownership more attainable for families across Arkansas and the nation... This legislation strengthens community banks, modernizes building codes, and cuts red tape. More houses will be built, more families will enter the market, and homes across the country will be more affordable.

As a former community banker in central Arkansas, I know how important our Main Street banks are to our local economy... It right-sizes regulations for our community banks, freeing them up to lend so entrepreneurs can invest, businesses can grow, and families can build wealth.

positions.summary: Sponsored the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, enacted in 2026, which he describes as reducing regulatory barriers to new home construction and modernizing local zoning rules to increase housing supply.
positions.quote: It cuts red tape, increases housing supply, and makes homeownership more attainable for families across Arkansas and the nation.

record.text: Currently serves on the House Committee on Financial Services and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
Sponsored the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a bipartisan housing bill that reduces regulatory barriers to home construction and modernizes HUD programs; signed into law in July 2026.
Sponsored the Main Street Capital Access Act (H.R. 6955), which right-sizes bank capital regulations for community banks; passed the House 270-155-1 in July 2026.

candidates.name: Chris Jones

summary.text: Chris Jones is the Democratic nominee for Arkansas's 2nd Congressional District. A physicist and ordained minister who grew up in Pine Bluff, he led the Arkansas Regional Innovation Hub before becoming the 2022 Democratic nominee for governor, a race he lost to Sarah Huckabee Sanders. He is running on lowering costs, healthcare access, economic opportunity and voting rights.

background.text: Born in Pine Bluff, Arkansas, the son of two preachers; he graduated from Watson Chapel High School.

Earned a B.S. in physics and mathematics from Morehouse College (1999), an M.S. in nuclear engineering/technology and policy from MIT (2003), and a Ph.D. in urban planning from MIT (2016); he says he attended Morehouse on a full NASA scholarship.
Career experience includes work as a nuclear engineer, physicist, minister and nonprofit leader; he describes himself as an ordained minister.

Says he returned to Arkansas to serve as Executive Director of the Arkansas Regional Innovation Hub, which he says he led for three years working on entrepreneurship, STEAM education and workforce training.
Won the May 24, 2022 Democratic primary for Arkansas governor over four opponents, then lost the general election to Republican Sarah Huckabee Sanders, 63% to 35%.
Announced his campaign for the 2nd District on October 9, 2025, and won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary over Zack Huffman.
Says he is married to a combat veteran and is the father of three girls.

priorities.text: Campaign site lists three pillars: "Affordability For All," "Accountability For All," and "Opportunity For All."
Describes his campaign as focused on expanding opportunity and strengthening communities, citing prior work on schools, jobs, and healthcare access.
priorities.quote: I'm a bridge builder, a fighter for us, and a visionary for the future of Arkansas. Our campaign is about expanding opportunity, strengthening our communities, and proving that when Arkansans come together, we can fly.

candidates.researchNotes: Jones has not completed a 2026 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey for this race; his Ballotpedia page's quoted policy platform dates to his 2022 gubernatorial campaign and was not used here as a current position. Specific 2026 issue positions were not found beyond his campaign site's three named priorities.
